transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I called because I’m having this thing at work where every little sudden noise is making me jump out of my skin. Like, it doesn’t even have to be something big—someone shuts a file drawer a little too hard, or a coffee mug gets dropped, or there’s just a sharp bang somewhere in the office—and I react like it’s something serious. My whole body jolts, and then my chest starts racing.

And the part that’s bothering me is it doesn’t just settle down right away. I’ll tell myself, “It was just a drawer, calm down,” but my heart keeps pounding way longer than it should, and I’m sitting there trying to act normal in front of everyone. It’s gotten embarrassing enough that I finally reached out through EAP, because it’s starting to feel like I can’t relax even in a normal office setting.
Outside of the noises at work, do you find yourself constantly on edge or unusually alert, like you’re always waiting for something bad to happen?

Yeah… I think that’s actually happening more than I wanted to admit. When I’m in the office now, I’m not just sitting there doing my job like normal. I keep sort of tracking everything around me, like where my boss is, if he’s coming down the row, whether someone’s walking up behind me, stuff like that.

And I know it sounds excessive, because it’s an office, not some dangerous place, but I’ll be trying to focus on my team or answer an email and part of my brain is still checking the exits, or looking over my shoulder if I hear footsteps. It’s like I can’t fully settle into the work. I’m there, but I’m also kind of… scanning the room all the time, waiting for something to happen.
Do you find yourself reacting this way to sudden noises or feeling on edge in places other than work, like at home or in public?

Mostly at work, honestly. That’s where I notice it the most, and that’s what finally pushed me to call EAP. It’s like every little bang in the office sets me off — a file drawer shutting too hard, someone dropping a coffee mug, even just a sharp noise from down the hall. I jump way harder than I should, like my whole body reacts before I can even think.

And then my chest keeps racing afterward, which is the part that bothers me. If it was just a quick startle, maybe I’d brush it off, but it lingers. I’m sitting there trying to look normal, like, “Okay, it was just a drawer,” but my body doesn’t seem to get the message right away.
Have you noticed yourself being more alert or reacting strongly to sudden noises even when you're not at work, like at home or in other public places?

I mean… not really in the same way, no. It’s mostly at work that it’s become impossible to ignore. That’s kind of what finally made me call EAP, because every little bang in the office feels like it hits me physically before I even have time to think.

Like, if a file drawer slams shut, or somebody drops a coffee mug, or there’s just some sharp noise nearby, I jump hard. Not just a normal little flinch — my whole body kind of jolts, and then my chest starts pounding. And the annoying part is it keeps going way longer than it should. I’ll be sitting there thinking, “Okay, it was just a drawer, you’re fine,” but my body is still acting like something happened.

So, I guess outside of work I haven’t noticed it as much, or at least it doesn’t stand out to me the same way. But in the office, yeah, that’s the main thing. That’s the thing that made me feel like I needed to talk to someone.
Have you found yourself avoiding certain places, people, or situations at work—or even outside of work—because you’re worried they might trigger one of these reactions or make you feel on edge?

I’m not sure I’d say I’m avoiding places exactly. I mean, not in a deliberate way like, “I can’t go there,” or “I refuse to be around that person.” I still go to work, I still sit where I’m supposed to sit, I still deal with the people I need to deal with.

I guess I do notice I’m more… careful? Like if I know there’s a spot in the office that tends to be louder, I’m not excited to be around it, but I don’t know that I’ve fully changed my routine around it. And outside of work, I haven’t really noticed myself avoiding anything. I’m not, like, skipping stores or restaurants because I think something will set me off.

So… I don’t think so, not really. It’s more that when I’m there, I feel tense, but I haven’t started avoiding whole places or people because of it.

When you're not at work—like when you're driving, at home, or out with friends—do you ever catch yourself being extra watchful or reacting more strongly to sudden sounds than you used to, even if it doesn’t make you avoid those places?

Not really when I’m out with friends or driving, at least not that I can clearly point to. I don’t find myself scanning restaurants or anything like that.

But at work, yeah… that part is definitely happening. I didn’t even really think of it as “watchful” until you said it that way, but I am constantly checking things in the office now. Like where my boss is, whether he’s coming down the aisle, who’s behind me, if someone’s walking up near my desk. I’ll catch myself looking toward the exits too, which feels kind of dramatic to say out loud, because I know I’m just in an office, not somewhere dangerous.

And I’m supposed to be focused on my team, you know? I’m supposed to be supervising, answering questions, staying on top of the numbers, that kind of thing. But part of my attention is always off to the side, tracking where people are or whether someone’s about to come up behind me. It’s distracting, and it makes me feel like I’m not fully there.
When you're not at work—like at home or in other everyday situations—do you ever notice yourself being more alert than you used to be, even if it's not as intense as what you feel in the office?

Not really at home, no… or at least I don’t notice it the same way. It’s hard because now that we’re talking about it, I keep second-guessing what counts as “more alert.” But the place where it really shows up is still the office.

Like, when I’m sitting at my desk, I’ll realize I’m not just working. Part of me is keeping tabs on everything around me — where my boss is, whether he’s walking near our area, whether someone is coming up behind me. I’ll look toward the exits more than I used to, too, which feels weird to admit because, I mean, it’s an office. I know where the doors are. I shouldn’t need to keep checking.

But I do. Even when I’m supposed to be focused on my team or answering questions, there’s this part of my attention that’s constantly sort of… scanning. At home, I don’t think I’m doing that in any obvious way. It’s mainly when I’m back in that work environment.
When you're at home or in other familiar, safe places, do you ever catch yourself being more alert or watchful than you used to be, even if it's not as intense as what you feel at work?

At home, no, not really in the same way. I mean, I don’t think I’m walking around my apartment checking corners or listening for every noise or anything like that. If I’m somewhere familiar, I can usually just be there.

It’s when I’m in the office that it happens. I keep catching myself checking where my boss is, like whether he’s near my area or walking down the aisle, and I’m also aware of where the exits are in a way I never used to be. And if someone comes up behind me, or I think someone might be coming up behind me, my attention goes right to that instead of whatever I’m supposed to be doing.

That’s the frustrating part, because I’m supposed to be focused on my team and what they need from me, but I’m partly watching the room the whole time. It feels excessive, but I keep doing it.
Have you ever felt unusually alert or had a strong reaction to sudden noises in places other than work, even if it wasn’t as intense as what you feel in the office?

Other than work… not really that I can think of. I don’t want to say “never,” because now I’m kind of overanalyzing myself, but I haven’t noticed it in the same clear way anywhere else.

In the office, though, it’s very obvious to me now. I’m constantly checking where my boss is, like if he’s walking near my desk or down the aisle, and I keep noticing where the exits are. I also get really aware of whether someone is coming up behind me, even if it’s just normal office movement. It pulls my attention away from what I’m supposed to be doing, like helping my team or staying on top of work stuff.

So outside of work, I can’t really point to that happening. At work, yes — that’s where I’m on edge and watching things much more than I used to.
Has anything happened at work recently—like a specific incident, confrontation, or stressful situation—that you think might be connected to why you're feeling this way in the office now?

I’m not sure. I mean, that’s the part I keep trying to line up in my head, because it feels like there should be one clear thing I can point to, like, “Yes, this happened and then I started feeling this way.” But I don’t know that I have that.

There have been stressful moments at work, sure, and I guess tension with my boss isn’t exactly new, but I don’t know if there was one specific confrontation or incident that explains why I’m suddenly so aware of him in the office. I keep replaying different interactions and wondering if I’m making too much of them or if there’s something I’m missing.

So… I don’t want to say there was nothing, because work has been stressful, but I can’t honestly give you a specific event and say, “That’s it.” I just know that being in the office feels different now, and I’m having a hard time figuring out exactly why.

Have you ever experienced or witnessed something at work that felt truly frightening or traumatic, even if it wasn’t physically harmful—like a serious argument, threat, or something that made you feel in danger?

Yeah… I mean, I guess there was something. I’ve been kind of avoiding calling it that, because it feels dramatic to say it was traumatic, but it did scare me.

There was this moment with my boss where he got really angry, and I remember certain parts of it very clearly. Like, I can still see him slamming the chair—hard enough that the sound kind of snapped through the room—and then he was standing in front of the door. Not just near it, like… in the way of it. And I remember thinking, “I can’t just leave.” Even though nothing physical happened to me, that part felt really bad.

But the weird thing is, when I try to explain the worst part, I can’t. I know he said something to me, and I know whatever he said is the part that made me feel the most scared or trapped, but the actual words are just blank. It’s like I can remember the chair, the door, his posture, how my body felt, all of that, but the sentence itself is gone. Like that section got cut out.

And I hate saying that because it sounds like I’m being vague on purpose, or like I’m trying to make it worse than it was, but I’m not. I’ve tried to replay it and put the words back in order, and I just can’t.

This supports the possibility of PTSD (F43.11). The persistence of symptoms only in the work environment, with hypervigilance, exaggerated startle response, and intrusive recollection of the event's sensory components, also supports F43.11. Complex PTSD (F43.12) remains a candidate due to the interpersonal nature and ongoing stress at work. Adjustment disorder with anxiety (F43.22) is ruled out due to the specificity and intensity of the trauma response, leaving F43.23 (adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood) as a broader, less specific alternative. Phobias (F40.0-2) and panic disorder (F41.0) were ruled out due to the situational specificity and trauma history.

doctor.question: Have you ever experienced or witnessed something at work that felt truly frightening or traumatic, even if it wasn’t physically harmful—like a serious argument, threat, or something that made you feel in danger?

target_item.name: Trauma_Related_Amnesia
target_item.manifestation: I remember him slamming the chair and standing in front of the door, but when I try to explain the worst part, the actual words he said to me are just blank, like that section got cut out.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a frightening or traumatic work incident; this profile item contains the traumatic confrontation details, including the boss slamming the chair, blocking the door, and a blank memory for the worst part.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, I guess there was something. I’ve been kind of avoiding calling it that, because it feels dramatic to say it was traumatic, but it did scare me.

There was this moment with my boss where he got really angry, and I remember certain parts of it very clearly. Like, I can still see him slamming the chair—hard enough that the sound kind of snapped through the room—and then he was standing in front of the door. Not just near it, like… in the way of it. And I remember thinking, “I can’t just leave.” Even though nothing physical happened to me, that part felt really bad.

But the weird thing is, when I try to explain the worst part, I can’t. I know he said something to me, and I know whatever he said is the part that made me feel the most scared or trapped, but the actual words are just blank. It’s like I can remember the chair, the door, his posture, how my body felt, all of that, but the sentence itself is gone. Like that section got cut out.

And I hate saying that because it sounds like I’m being vague on purpose, or like I’m trying to make it worse than it was, but I’m not. I’ve tried to replay it and put the words back in order, and I just can’t.

inference.note: The patient described a traumatic experience at work involving their boss, including physical intimidation (blocking the door, slamming a chair) and an inability to recall the exact words spoken, despite remembering the physical and emotional sensations vividly. This supports the possibility of PTSD (F43.11). The persistence of symptoms only in the work environment, with hypervigilance, exaggerated startle response, and intrusive recollection of the event's sensory components, also supports F43.11. Complex PTSD (F43.12) remains a candidate due to the interpersonal nature and ongoing stress at work. Adjustment disorder with anxiety (F43.22) is ruled out due to the specificity and intensity of the trauma response, leaving F43.23 (adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood) as a broader, less specific alternative. Phobias (F40.0-2) and panic disorder (F41.0) were ruled out due to the situational specificity and trauma history.
